author: Claude (English teacher role), v2 against the v2 quality gate
basis: Full rewrite. The previous overlay kept most of the workbook A2 column, which sat above the A2 band on Flesch-Kincaid and long-word load on seven slides and ran over the 20-second clock on three. This version is written from the source meaning, slide by slide, in present-simple spoken English with one idea per sentence, and it shares almost no content words with the B1 and B2 texts, so the three levels are three texts rather than one text in three coats. Meaning, slide order and every named fact are unchanged: SDG 9 Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure; ChatGPT; Gemini; AI hallucination; Google Scholar; PubMed. Technical corrections: the workbook A2 says AI 'only guesses the next word' and that 'sometimes the formulas and data are completely wrong'. A language model predicts the most likely next word from patterns in the text it was trained on, and what it fabricates is sources, not arithmetic, so those lines are restated as prediction and as invented sources. Nothing here says the model knows, understands or looks anything up.

slides.1: Good morning. Today I talk about SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure. It asks every country in the world to make things well and to try new ideas.
slides.2: Now AI is a strong new engine inside science. It reads data very quickly and offers ideas to any researcher in a second. But can we trust the answer?
slides.3: Many science students use ChatGPT or Gemini every day. We write lab reports with it, and it makes hard ideas clear. It is quick, and it saves us time.
slides.4: But AI is not always right. It can invent papers, authors and facts that do not exist. We call this AI hallucination, and it sounds very real.
slides.5: Why does this happen? A model never studies science, because it only copies the habits of writing on the Internet. It offers the word that usually comes next.
slides.6: So the answer can sound perfect and still be wrong. The model never opens a journal or a textbook. Smooth English is simply not the same as truth.
slides.7: What happens if we copy those empty titles into a lab report? We may fail the paper. Even worse, nobody trusts a future scientist who never checks.
slides.8: The danger is bigger than my degree. People slowly stop believing science when wrong facts travel fast. Nothing new can help a public that trusts nobody.
slides.9: So what can we do? First, never treat an AI answer as the final word. Stop for a moment, and ask a simple question: is this really true?
slides.10: Second, check every title yourself before you trust it. Try a trusted site like Google Scholar or PubMed. A machine can search fast, but the choice stays ours.
slides.11: Even today, your human voice still matters. A computer can copy and arrange data forever. But it feels no wonder, and it never worries about right or wrong.
slides.12: AI is one famous invention of SDG 9. But a clever tool without honest people is just a factory of lies. Machines arrange the words, and we find the truth.
